person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: The results indicate that music influenced customers' product selections.

span.label: musical fit and in-store product choice
span.quote: This field study investigated the extent to which stereotypically French and German music could influence supermarket customers' selections of French and German wines.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: French and German music was played on alternate days alongside French and German wines in the alcoholic beverages section of a supermarket.

span.label: Whether shoppers were genuinely unaware of the influence is undetermined; they may have realised it but declined to admit it
span.quote: Second, it remains to be determined whether customers really were unaware of the effects of music on their purchasing: Maybe customers did realize that the music was an attempt to influence their purchasing, but did not like to admit this to researchers.

span.label: The alternative that the music merely attracted already-decided buyers to the display cannot be ruled out
span.quote: The present data does not allow us to test this alternative explanation.

span.label: The preference-for-prototypes model invoked to explain the effect was not itself tested
span.quote: It should be noted that the present research does not attempt to test the preference-forprototypes model directly.

span.label: musical fit
span.quote: The most obvious explanation for this is simply that the effects of musical fit on product selection are not consciously recognised, which raises three points

span.label: knowledge
span.quote: the finding is consistent with the notion that music can prime related knowledge and the selection of certain products if they fit with that knowledge

span.label: uncertainty
span.quote: suggests that the heuristic influence of music would mediate behavior only when there is an element of uncertainty in product choice or when customers are in a state of low involvement with the decision process

span.label: low involvement
span.quote: suggests that the heuristic influence of music would mediate behavior only when there is an element of uncertainty in product choice or when customers are in a state of low involvement with the decision process

span.label: THE AUTHORS TAKE APART THEIR OWN EVIDENCE FOR UNAWARENESS, IN THREE MOVES. First the hedge is built into the report: `TAKEN PURELY AT FACE VALUE, the questionnaire data suggest that respondents were largely unaware of the effect that music had on their wine selections.` Then: `it REMAINS TO BE DETERMINED whether customers really were unaware ...: MAYBE CUSTOMERS DID REALIZE that the music was an attempt to influence their purchasing, BUT DID NOT LIKE TO ADMIT THIS to researchers.` **A self-report of unawareness is treated as evidence about what people will SAY**, which is a different quantity from what they knew - and most awareness checks in this corpus are reported as measurements of the second
span.quote: Second, it remains to be determined whether customers really were unaware of the effects of music on their purchasing: Maybe customers did realize that the music was an attempt to influence their purchasing, but did not like to admit this to researchers

span.label: AND THE THIRD MOVE IS SUBTLER THAN IMPRESSION MANAGEMENT: `customers may not have explained their wine choice in terms of the music simply because THIS DID NOT SEEM TO THEM LIKE A RATIONAL EXPLANATION for their behavior.` Not concealment and not ignorance - a FOLK THEORY OF WHAT COUNTS AS A REASON. A shopper who half-noticed the music may still not offer it, because `the music was playing` is not the kind of thing that explains a purchase. So a null on a `why did you choose this` question is evidence about the respondent's model of explanation, and only then about awareness
span.quote: Indeed, customers may not have explained their wine choice in terms of the music simply because this did not seem to them like a rational explanation for their behavior

span.label: THE SAME BOUNDARY CONDITION money2013 GIVES, SIXTEEN YEARS EARLIER AND IN A DIFFERENT FIELD. Here: the effect holds `ONLY WHEN THERE IS AN ELEMENT OF UNCERTAINTY in product choice or when customers are in a state of LOW INVOLVEMENT with the decision process`. Vohs's 2015 reply to a failed replication says priming needs an AMBIGUOUS OUTCOME - `a situation that does not leave much room for interpretation is unlikely to show a consistent or large priming effect`. **Marketing in 1999 and social psychology in 2015, arriving independently at the condition that a prime needs somewhere to act**, and each citing its own literature (judgmental biases here, Loersch & Payne there)
span.quote: suggests that the heuristic influence of music would mediate behavior only when there is an element of uncertainty in product choice or when customers are in a state of low involvement with the decision process

span.label: AN ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION THE DATA CANNOT RULE OUT, STATED WITHOUT DEFENCE - AND THEN A REPLY THAT COSTS NOTHING. `Because the music was played FROM THE DISPLAY containing the wines, it may well have ATTRACTED THE ATTENTION of people who already intended to buy wine from one of the countries in question ... The present data does not allow us to test this alternative explanation.` The concession is total. The reply is that it does not matter: `even if this alternative explanation is correct ... the fact that music was able to attract them to a specific area of the store STILL SHOWS that music activated knowledge and was associated with the selection of matching products.` **The mechanism claim survives the confound because both routes require the same activation**
span.quote: Second, even if this alternative explanation is correct in the case of some customers, then the fact that music was able to attract them to a specific area of the store still shows that music activated knowledge and was associated with the selection of matching products

span.label: builds-on → Areni and Kim (1993)
span.quote: This theoretical framework has interesting parallels with Areni and Kim's (1993) arguments concerning musical fit and product selection discussed earlier.

span.label: builds-on → Martindale and Moore's (1988) preference-for-prototypes model
span.quote: Although the aim of Martindale and Moore's (1988) model is to explain preferences between aesthetic objects, it is relevant to consumer research because it suggests the role of knowledge activation in responses to music.

span.label: knowledge —part-of→ musical fit
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — THE MECHANISM PREDICTION, and the type is the nearest the vocabulary has rather than the right one: what the paper claims is that musical fit WORKS THROUGH knowledge activation, and the eight types have no term for `works through`. `part-of` reads it as the activation being a constituent of the effect, which is the sense the sentence supports - `music should PRIME certain aspects of consumers' knowledge ... SUCH THAT the effects of musical fit ... can be explained`. Weight 0.8: `should` is a prediction, and this span is from the introduction rather than the results.
span.quote: In-store music should prime certain aspects of consumers' knowledge of the world and increase their likelihood of selecting appropriate products, such that the effects of musical fit on product choice can be explained in terms of the preference for prototypes model

span.label: shoppers are largely unaware of the musics influence on their choice
span.quote: Responses to a questionnaire suggested that customers were unaware of these effects of music on their product choices.
